rules.statement: Never write secret material to an audit record: no token or refresh token value, credential, key material, wrapped key, key check, cookie value, session handle, `state`, authorization code or initial access token. Write identifiers and non-sensitive metadata (such as `kid`, token type, claim names) instead.
rules.why: Audit records go to logs, traces and custom sinks. The catalog lists for each event what may be written and states that no token, credential or key material is ever written.
rules.check: Look at new or changed audit event constructions and `details` and `resource_values` payloads for any token value, secret, key bytes, cookie, code or credential, including in snapshots of resources.

rules.statement: Publish an audit event for a state change only after the change has committed, so a change that a lost race or rollback discarded is never recorded.
rules.why: The audit trail must record only changes that actually took effect.
rules.check: Look for audit events published before the persistence commit or concurrency check, or published on a path where the write can still fail or be discarded.

rules.statement: Put only a verified subject or client identifier in an audit record's subject id field. Record an unverified user name the request presented in a separate details member, such as `attempted_username`, and leave the subject id absent.
rules.why: This keeps `subject_id` trustworthy, so it only ever holds a verified subject id.
rules.check: On failure paths, such as refused credentials, look for request-supplied user names or ids being assigned to the subject id field of an audit event.

rules.statement: Don't use unbounded values such as a tenant, client, subject or network address as metric attributes. Use only bounded vocabularies such as event name, category and outcome.
rules.why: Only bounded fields may be metric attributes, which keeps metric cardinality bounded.
rules.check: Look at tags added to counters and histograms for identifiers, user data or addresses.

rules.statement: When flattening structured event data into log state or span tags, flatten only one level of nested details. Emit arrays and deeper nested values as raw JSON text, omit null members, and keep JSON numbers as numbers.
rules.why: This bounds the number of index fields one event can create and keeps the numeric fields queryable as numbers.
rules.check: Look at log-state or span-tag flattening code that recurses into arrays or nested objects, emits keys for nulls, or turns numbers into strings.

rules.statement: Dispatch observation and audit event handlers so that a handler that throws neither fails the audited operation nor stops the other handlers from running.
rules.why: Observation is a fault-isolated seam: a broken sink must not break the protocol operation or the other sinks.
rules.check: Look for event dispatch that lets handler exceptions propagate to the caller or stop the loop over handlers.

rules.statement: Capture the request context when an event is published, not when its handler runs, so a handler running in the background after the request has completed still sees it.
rules.why: Sinks may run after the request completes, when the HttpContext is no longer valid.
rules.check: Look for event handlers that read `IHttpContextAccessor` or the ambient request state at handling time instead of reading the context captured on the event.
